q: Click any member of NATO.
f: NATO was founded in 1949. Finland joined in 2023 and Sweden in 2024, bringing it to 32 members.

q: Click any of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
f: The five are the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China, and each holds a veto.

q: Click any of the five nuclear-weapon states recognized by the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
f: They are the same five countries that hold permanent Security Council seats.

q: Click the country that hosts the United Nations headquarters.
f: The UN headquarters in New York City opened in 1952.

q: Click the only country that has used nuclear weapons in war.
f: The United States bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

q: Click the country that hosts NATO's headquarters.
f: NATO's headquarters are in Brussels.

q: Click the country that Russia invaded in February 2022.
f: The full-scale invasion began on February 24, 2022.

q: Click either of the two countries formed from the divided Korean Peninsula.
f: The peninsula was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945, and the Korean War (1950-53) ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty.

q: Click the country that left the European Union in 2020.
f: The UK left on January 31, 2020, after a 2016 referendum.

q: Click any member of the G7.
f: The G7 countries are the U.S., U.K., France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada, and the EU also takes part.

q: Click the country where the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
f: They took Kabul in August 2021 as U.S. forces withdrew.

q: Click the island nation at the center of the 1962 missile crisis.
f: Soviet missiles in Cuba triggered a 13-day standoff between the U.S. and the USSR.

q: Click the country with the world's largest military budget.
f: U.S. defense spending exceeds that of the next several countries combined.

q: Click the world's most populous country, as of 2023.
f: India passed China in 2023, according to the United Nations.

q: Find the Suez Canal, which links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
f: Roughly 12 percent of global trade passes through it.

q: Find the Panama Canal, which links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
f: It opened in 1914, and the U.S. handed control to Panama at the end of 1999.

q: Find the Strait of Gibraltar, the gateway into the Mediterranean.
f: It is only about 14 km wide at its narrowest point.

q: Click any member of the European Union.
f: The EU has 27 members. Malta is a member too, but it's too small to appear on this map.

q: Click any member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.
f: The alliance traces back to the 1946 UKUSA Agreement.

q: Click any of the three countries outside the five recognized nuclear powers that have tested nuclear weapons.
f: India tested in 1974 and 1998, Pakistan in 1998 and North Korea starting in 2006.

q: Click the country that joined NATO in 2023.
f: It ended decades of military non-alignment after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

q: Click the newest NATO member, which joined in March 2024.
f: Sweden's accession followed Finland's, after Turkey and Hungary ratified.

q: Click the country that hosts the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
f: Both are in The Hague.

q: Click the country that hosts the International Atomic Energy Agency.
f: The IAEA is headquartered in Vienna.

q: Click the country that Iraq invaded in 1990.
f: A U.S.-led coalition liberated Kuwait in early 1991.

q: Click the country whose 1979 revolution created an Islamic republic.
f: The Shah fled in January 1979 and Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile.

q: Click the Mediterranean island divided since 1974.
f: A UN buffer zone, the Green Line, separates the Greek-Cypriot south from the Turkish-controlled north.

q: Click the country that fought a 1982 war with Britain over the Falkland Islands.
f: The war lasted 74 days and ended in Argentine defeat.

q: Click the country created in 1947 as a Muslim-majority state when British India was partitioned.
f: Bangladesh split from Pakistan in 1971.

q: Click the Central African country where a 1994 genocide killed an estimated 800,000 people.
f: It lasted about 100 days.

q: Click the country that claimed to annex Crimea in 2014, a move most countries reject.
f: The UN General Assembly voted to affirm Ukraine's territorial integrity.

q: Click the NATO member that controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits.
f: The 1936 Montreux Convention gives Turkey control over warship passage.

q: Find the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world's oil exports pass.
f: It is only about 33 km wide at its narrowest.

q: Find the Bosporus, the strait that splits Istanbul and links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara.
f: Turkey controls it under the 1936 Montreux Convention.

q: Find the Strait of Malacca, which links the Indian and Pacific oceans.
f: Roughly a quarter of world trade sails through it.

q: Find the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
f: It separates England from France and is about 33 km wide at the Strait of Dover.

q: Click the host of Camp Lemonnier, the only permanent U.S. military base in Africa.
f: It sits at the mouth of the Red Sea near Bab-el-Mandeb.

q: Click the NATO member that borders Iran, Iraq and Syria.
f: Turkey also borders Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Greece and Bulgaria.

q: Click the NATO member that borders Russia's Kaliningrad exclave to the south.
f: Lithuania borders it to the north and east.

q: Click the country that left NATO's integrated military command in 1966 and rejoined in 2009.
f: President de Gaulle took France out but kept it in the alliance itself.

q: Click the newest member of the European Union, which joined in 2013.
f: Croatia also joined the euro and the Schengen area in 2023.

q: Click either country divided by the Kashmir Line of Control.
f: Both claim all of Kashmir, and China holds part of the region too.

q: Click the country that hosts Europe's largest nuclear power plant, at Zaporizhzhia.
f: Russian forces seized the plant in March 2022.

q: Click any of the three former Soviet republics that gave up inherited nuclear weapons in the 1990s.
f: They transferred their Soviet-era warheads to Russia.

q: Click the country whose war ended with the 1995 Dayton Accords.
f: The accords were negotiated at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio.

q: Click the country where the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster occurred.
f: It was then part of the Soviet Union.

q: Click the country that hosts Ramstein Air Base, a hub of U.S. military power in Europe.
f: Ramstein is home to U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa.

q: Click the country that leases the Baikonur Cosmodrome to Russia.
f: Baikonur launched Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1.

q: Click the world's largest producer of uranium.
f: It produces more than a third of the world's mined uranium.

q: Find Bab-el-Mandeb, the strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
f: Attacks on ships since late 2023 have pushed many vessels to sail around Africa.

q: Find the Taiwan Strait.
f: It is about 180 km wide at its narrowest.

q: Find the Danish Straits, which guard the entrance to the Baltic Sea.
f: Denmark controls them, and ships pass through the Oresund and the Great Belt.

q: Find the Cape of Good Hope, the route around Africa.
f: Ships use it when the Suez Canal or Red Sea is closed or unsafe.

q: Find the Korea Strait, between South Korea and Japan.
f: The Tsushima Islands divide it into two channels.

q: Click the country that formally left the Warsaw Pact in 1968.
f: It had broken with the Soviet Union in 1961 and sided with China.

q: Click the only country to have voluntarily dismantled its home-built nuclear weapons.
f: It destroyed six devices and joined the NPT in 1991.

q: Click the country whose 1956 uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks.
f: Thousands died and about 200,000 people fled.

q: Click either country that was once Czechoslovakia, where the 1968 Prague Spring was crushed.
f: The two split peacefully in 1993.

q: Click the Nordic country that hosted the 1975 conference that produced the Helsinki Final Act.
f: Finland's neutrality made it a natural host.

q: Click the country that hosts the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons.
f: The OPCW sits in The Hague and won the 2013 Nobel Peace Prize.

q: Click the country whose Arctic territory hosts Thule Air Base, the northernmost U.S. military base.
f: The base, now called Pituffik Space Base, is in Greenland, a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

q: Click the country that hosts the Aviano and Sigonella air bases.
f: Both are important to U.S. and NATO air operations in the Mediterranean.

q: Click the country divided along the 17th parallel in 1954.
f: The Geneva Accords split it into North and South.

q: Click the country that hosts Pine Gap, a joint U.S.-Australian satellite ground station.
f: Pine Gap is near Alice Springs in the Northern Territory.

q: Click the Nordic country that hosted the 1986 Reagan-Gorbachev summit.
f: They met in Reykjavik and nearly agreed to abolish nuclear weapons.

q: Click the country that governs Svalbard under a 1920 treaty.
f: The treaty lets signatory countries mine and do business there, but forbids military bases.

q: Click the country that hosted the 1943 Tehran Conference of Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.
f: It was the first meeting of the three together.

q: Click the country that hosted the 1945 Potsdam Conference.
f: Truman, Stalin and Churchill (later Attlee) met near Berlin.

q: Find the Lombok Strait, a deep-water alternative to the Strait of Malacca.
f: Large tankers can pass through it, and it runs between Bali and Lombok.

q: Find the Kerch Strait, between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
f: A bridge across it, built after Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, is a contested symbol.

q: Click one of the 12 founding members of NATO (1949).
f: NATO was founded in Washington on 4 April 1949 by 12 countries in Europe and North America.

q: Click one of the six founding members of the European Communities (1957 Treaty of Rome).
f: The "Inner Six" signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957; West Germany is today's Germany.

q: Click one of the four original BRIC countries.
f: BRIC held its first summit in 2009; South Africa joined in 2010, making it BRICS.

q: Click a country that joined NATO in 1999, the first enlargement after the Cold War.
f: The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined on 12 March 1999.

q: Click a country that joined NATO in the big 2004 enlargement.
f: Seven countries joined in March 2004, including the three Baltic states.

q: Click a country that joined the EU in the 2004 enlargement.
f: Ten countries joined on 1 May 2004; the tenth, Malta, is too small for this map.

q: Click a country that joined BRICS at the start of 2024.
f: Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined in January 2024; Saudi Arabia was invited and Indonesia joined in 2025.

q: Click a founding member of ASEAN (1967).
f: ASEAN was founded in Bangkok in 1967; the fifth founder, Singapore, is too small for this map.

q: Click the country that joined BRICS in 2010.
f: South Africa joined in December 2010, turning BRIC into BRICS.

q: Click a country that joined the European Communities in 1973, the first enlargement.
f: Denmark, Ireland and the UK joined on 1 January 1973; Norway's voters said no.

q: Click a country that joined the EU in 1995.
f: Austria, Finland and Sweden joined on 1 January 1995.

q: Click a country that joined the EU in 2007.
f: Bulgaria and Romania joined on 1 January 2007.

q: Click a country that joined NATO in 1952, its first enlargement.
f: Greece and Turkey joined in February 1952.

q: Click a country that joined NATO in 2009.
f: Albania and Croatia joined on 1 April 2009.

q: Click a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
f: The GCC was founded in 1981; its sixth member, Bahrain, is too small for this map.

q: Click a founding member of Mercosur (1991).
f: The Treaty of Asunción created Mercosur in 1991; Bolivia became a full member in 2024.

q: Click a founding member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (2001).
f: The SCO grew out of the "Shanghai Five" plus Uzbekistan; India and Pakistan joined in 2017.

q: Click a founding member of OPEC (1960).
f: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by five oil producers.

q: Click the country that joined NATO in 1955 (then as West Germany).
f: West Germany joined in May 1955; days later the Soviet bloc founded the Warsaw Pact.

q: Click the country that joined NATO in 1982.
f: Spain joined in 1982, seven years after Franco's death, and confirmed it in a 1986 referendum.

q: Click a country that joined the European Communities in 1981 or 1986.
f: Greece joined in 1981, Spain and Portugal in 1986, after each had left dictatorship behind.

q: Click a country that joined NATO in 2017 or 2020.
f: Montenegro joined in 2017 and North Macedonia in 2020, after settling its name dispute with Greece.

q: Click one of the four African founding members of the United Nations (1945).
f: Only four of the 51 founding members were in Africa; most of the continent was still colonised.

q: Click the home country of a leader who launched the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.
f: Tito (Yugoslavia, from Belgrade), Nehru, Nasser, Nkrumah and Sukarno led the 1961 Belgrade summit.

q: Find the city that hosts NATO's headquarters.
f: NATO has been based in Brussels since 1967, after France left its integrated command.

q: Find the city that hosts the headquarters of the United Nations.
f: The UN headquarters on Manhattan's East River opened in 1952.

q: Find the city where the International Court of Justice sits.
f: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace; the International Criminal Court is also in The Hague.

q: Find the city that hosts the UN's European headquarters and the Red Cross.
f: Geneva hosts the UN Office, the WHO, the WTO and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

q: Find the city that hosts the International Atomic Energy Agency and OPEC.
f: Vienna also hosts the OSCE and one of the UN's four main offices.

q: Find the city that hosts the African Union's headquarters.
f: The AU, and the OAU before it since 1963, is based in Addis Ababa.

q: Find the city that hosts the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights.
f: Strasbourg is also the official seat of the European Parliament.

q: Find the city that hosts the OECD and UNESCO.
f: The OECD grew out of the body that ran the Marshall Plan.

q: Find the city that hosts the IMF and the World Bank.
f: Both were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference.

q: Find the city that hosts ASEAN's secretariat.
f: The ASEAN Secretariat has been in Jakarta since 1976.

q: Find the city that hosts the Arab League's headquarters.
f: The Arab League was founded in Cairo in 1945 (it moved to Tunis from 1979 to 1990).

q: Find the city that hosts the European Central Bank.
f: The ECB has set monetary policy for the euro from Frankfurt since 1998.

q: Find the city that hosts the UN Food and Agriculture Organization.
f: Rome also hosts the World Food Programme.

q: Find the city that hosts the UN Environment Programme.
f: UNEP, founded in 1972, was the first UN agency based in the Global South.

q: Find the city that hosts the Bank for International Settlements.
f: The BIS, founded in 1930, is the central bank for central banks.

q: Find the city that hosts the International Civil Aviation Organization.
f: ICAO was set up by the 1944 Chicago Convention.

q: Find the city that hosts the Gulf Cooperation Council's secretariat.
f: The GCC was founded in 1981, during the Iran-Iraq War.

q: Find the city that hosts Mercosur's secretariat.
f: Uruguay's capital hosts the Mercosur secretariat and parliament.

q: Which treaty drew this line through South America?
f: Spain and Portugal split the newly found lands along this meridian, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese.

q: Which secret agreement drew this line across the Middle East?
f: Britain and France divided the Ottoman Arab lands into zones "from the e in Acre to the last k in Kirkuk".

q: Which agreement set this line dividing Korea?
f: The armistice stopped the fighting along the front line; no peace treaty has ever been signed.

q: Which treaty set most of the border between the United States and Mexico?
f: Mexico gave up about half its territory; the 1853 Gadsden Purchase added the southern strip of Arizona and New Mexico.

q: Which conference agreed on this eastern border of Poland, close to the Curzon Line?
f: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed at Yalta to move Poland's eastern border west, roughly to the 1919 Curzon Line.

q: Which agreement moved this border west to the Oder and Neisse rivers?
f: Potsdam placed German lands east of the Oder-Neisse line under Polish administration; Germany finally confirmed the border in 1990.

q: Which line, drawn in five weeks, partitioned British India?
f: Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, drew the borders of Punjab and Bengal; they were published two days after independence.

q: Which agreement drew this border between Afghanistan and Pakistan?
f: British India and the Emir of Afghanistan agreed the line in 1893; Afghanistan has never formally recognised it.

q: Which treaty extended the 49th parallel border to the Pacific?
f: Britain and the United States split the Oregon Country, ending the "Fifty-four forty or fight!" dispute.

q: Which treaty fixed Hungary's borders, leaving it about a third of its former size?
f: Trianon left millions of ethnic Hungarians in neighbouring countries, a grievance that shaped interwar politics.

q: Which treaty arranged the 1920 vote that moved this border south?
f: Under Versailles, North Schleswig voted in 1920 to return to Denmark, setting today's border.

q: Which treaty set the 49th parallel as the border from Lake of the Woods to the Rockies?
f: The Anglo-American Convention of 1818 also left the Oregon Country under joint occupation.

q: Which treaty set this border between Turkey and Greece?
f: Lausanne replaced the harsher Treaty of Sèvres and set the Maritsa (Evros) river as the border in Thrace.

q: Which treaty set the borders of the new Republic of Austria?
f: Saint-Germain broke up the Austrian half of the Habsburg empire and forbade union with Germany.

q: Which agreement set the 22nd parallel as this border?
f: Britain and Egypt agreed to rule Sudan jointly, with the 22nd parallel as its northern limit.

q: Which treaties moved this border to the Amur and Ussuri rivers?
f: Qing China ceded the lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, where Vladivostok was founded in 1860.

q: Which agreement drew this border along the Panj river and the Wakhan Corridor?
f: Britain and Russia left the thin Wakhan Corridor to Afghanistan as a buffer between their empires.

q: Which treaty finally settled this border, returning Tacna to Peru?
f: Ending the dispute left by the War of the Pacific, Tacna went back to Peru and Arica stayed Chilean.

q: Which treaty cut Bulgaria off from the Aegean Sea along this border?
f: Bulgaria lost Western Thrace to Greece after siding with the Central Powers.

q: Which treaty set this border of Turkey with Armenia and Georgia?
f: Signed by Turkey and the three Soviet Transcaucasian republics, it left Kars and Ardahan in Turkey.

q: Which treaty returned Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria, setting this border?
f: Romania had taken Southern Dobruja in 1913; Germany pressed it to hand the region back in 1940.
